THE DESIGN.  `core_euclid_strict` is a combinational circuit with 22 input pins
u0..u10 and v0..v10, each a 3-bit two's-complement integer (so every coordinate
is in -4..3), one `valid` input, and three output pins: certified, refuted,
refused.  With valid = 1 exactly one output is high.  It decides whether two
integer vectors in Z^11 meet at an angle of at least 60 degrees:

    p = u.v   s = u.u   t = v.v            (three dot-product adder trees)
    in_box    = every coordinate satisfies -3 <= x <= 3   (the code point -4 is
                outside the declared box, and an out-of-box pair is REFUSED)
    certified = in_box and ( p <= 0  or  4*p^2 <= s*t )
    refuted   = in_box and   p > 0  and  4*p^2 >  s*t
    refused   = not in_box   (the datapath itself is complete: with 8-bit
                operands no in-box pair is ever refused for width)

Inside: each of the 22 products x*y is a 3x3-bit signed multiplier; the three
sums run through chains of adders (p is 10 bits signed, s and t are 9 bits
unsigned).  If p <= 0 the trivial branch certifies without the comparator.
Otherwise la = lb = 2p (8-bit unsigned, so 4p^2 = la*lb) and ra = s, rb = t go
to a comparator submodule `cmp` that forms lp = la*lb and rp = ra*rb (16 bits
each) and fires le = (lp <= rp) or gt = (lp > rp).  A `wide` flag fires if any
comparator operand is >= 256; no in-box pair reaches it.

Fourteen million certified pair verdicts from finished mathematics were run
against this netlist and could not see some of its mutants: every vector in
that corpus has u.u = v.v = 4, so any defect that only shows when the norms
differ, or when a coordinate is out of the box, or when |u.v| is near its
maximum of 99, is invisible to it.

## Understanding the Mutation

The mutation inverts bit 5 of input A in the AND-reduce operation. Looking at the netlist:
- `$116` is one bit of the 22-bit AND reduction for `ok` (which checks `in_box`)
- `$116 = $114 & $115` where:
  - `$114 = signed(v5) >= signed(3'h5)` 
  - `$115 = signed(v5) <= signed(3'h3)`

The mutation inverts bit 5 of input A. Since `$116` is 1 bit and sits at position in the reduction, "bit 5 of input A" refers to bit 5 of the AND-reduce's input, which is `$116` itself (the 6th bit, 0-indexed).

Wait, let me reconsider. The AND-reduce has 22 one-bit inputs. Bit 5 (0-indexed) would be the 6th input, which is `$116`.

The mutation: **bit 0 of `$116` is inverted** (since `$116` is 1 bit, bit 0 is its only bit).

This means: `$116` value is flipped.

`$116` checks: `(v5 >= 5) & (v5 <= 3)` which is always FALSE for valid 3-bit values.

The AND-reduce computes `ok` which should be TRUE when ALL coordinates are in box [-3, 3]. The mutation flips one bit of this reduction.

If the original `ok` should be TRUE (all coordinates in box), the mutation makes it FALSE.
If the original `ok` should be FALSE (some coordinate out of box), the mutation might make it TRUE.

The condition for `ok` depends on ALL 11 coordinates from u and v being in [-3, 3]. The `$116` term checks `(v5 >= 5) & (v5 <= 3)` which is a redundant/dead check (always false since v5 is 3-bit: range -4..3).

Actually, this is checking if v5 is simultaneously >= 5 AND <= 3, which is impossible. This term should always be 0 (FALSE).

With the inversion, this term becomes 1 (TRUE) instead of 0.

- All coordinates ARE in the box (original: `ok=TRUE`)
- With mutation, `ok` becomes FALSE
- This affects the output

- v5 in [-3, 3] (in box)
- All other coordinates in [-3, 3] (in box)
- The mutation of this one AND bit flips `ok` from TRUE to FALSE
- This changes the output

Any valid pair with all coordinates in [-3, 3] will have the original `ok=TRUE`. The mutation makes it `FALSE`, causing `refused` to become TRUE and `certified`/`refuted` to become FALSE.

refused.  With valid = 1 exactly one output is high.  It decides whether two
integer vectors in Z^11 meet at an angle of at least 60 degrees:

    p = u.v   s = u.u   t = v.v            (three dot-product adder trees)

                outside the declared box, and an out-of-box pair is REFUSED)

u0..u10 and v0..v10, each a 3-bit two's-complement integer (so every coordinate
is in -4..3), one `valid` input, and three output pins: certified, refuted,
refused.  With valid = 1 exactly one output is high.  It decides whether two
integer vectors in Z^11 meet at an angle of at least 60 degrees:

    p = u.v   s = u.u   t = v.v            (three dot-product adder trees)
    in_box    = every coordinate satisfies -3 <= x <= 3   (the code point -4 is
                outside the declared box, and an out-of-box pair is REFUSED)
    certified = in_box and ( p <= 0  or  4*p^2 <= s*t )
    refuted   = in_box and   p > 0  and  4*p^2 >  s*t
    refused   = not in_box   (the datapath itself is complete: with 8-bit
                operands no in-box pair is ever refused for width)

Inside: each of the 22 products x*y is a 3x3-bit signed multiplier; the three
sums run through chains of adders (p is 10 bits signed, s and t are 9 bits
unsigned).  If p <= 0 the trivial branch certifies without the comparator.
Otherwise la = lb = 2p (8-bit unsigned, so 4p^2 = la*lb) and ra = s, rb = t go
to a comparator submodule `cmp` that forms lp = la*lb and rp = ra*rb (16 bits
each) and fires le = (lp <= rp) or gt = (lp > rp).  A `wide` flag fires if any
comparator operand is >= 256; no in-box pair reaches it.

Fourteen million certified pair verdicts from finished mathematics were run
against this netlist and could not see some of its mutants: every vector in
that corpus has u.u = v.v = 4, so any defect that only shows when the norms
differ, or when a coordinate is out of the box, or when |u.v| is near its
maximum of 99, is invisible to it.

THE TASK.  One mutation may have been applied to this netlist -- a single bit of a
single cell's port bent -- or none at all.  Name one to eight input pairs (u, v) on
which the mutant's three output pins differ from the original's, or answer
EQUIVALENT if no input pair with valid = 1 can tell them apart, or UNDECIDED.

  wire widths:                    $129 is 1 bit
  (in the netlist, $N are internal wires; $signed(x) reads x as two's complement;
   in a concatenation { a, b, ..., z } the LEFTMOST element is the highest bit;

The mutation forces bit 2 of input B in a comparator to constant 0. Looking at the netlist line:
```
assign $129 = $signed(v10) >= $signed(3'h5);
```

However, the mutation forces bit 2 of the B input to 0. The constant `3'h5` in binary is `101` (bits 2, 1, 0). Forcing bit 2 to 0 changes it to `001` (which is 1).

- Original: `v10 >= 5` is always false (since v10 ∈ [-4, 3])

1. v10 ∈ {1, 2, 3} (to trigger the mutated condition)
2. The pair would otherwise be certified or refuted in the original
